_readme: Sidecar metadata for files whose .java source carries no problem statement.
Merged OVER parsed output by tools/generate.mjs. Your .java files are never modified.
Anything supplied from here is labelled 'generated' in the UI so you can always tell
it apart from your own words. Edit freely — your text wins over anything derived.
Keys are repo-relative paths. Fields: title, ids, url, statement, teaches, complexity, notes.
Run `node tools/generate.mjs --stubs` to print a skeleton for newly-added gap files.

src/Recursion/Factorial.java.statement: Compute n! using recursion. The recursive definition is n! = n x (n-1)!, with 0! = 1! = 1 as the base case.
src/Recursion/Factorial.java.teaches: The canonical first recursion: a single base case and one recursive call that strictly shrinks the input. Note the return type is long — 21! already overflows a 64-bit integer, so this also shows why you check the value range before choosing a type.
src/Recursion/Factorial.java.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the call stack.

src/Recursion/SumOfdigits.java.statement: Return the sum of the decimal digits of a non-negative integer, using recursion rather than a loop.
src/Recursion/SumOfdigits.java.teaches: Digit peeling with n % 10 to read the last digit and n / 10 to drop it. The base case is n == 0. This decomposition underlies most recursive number problems.
src/Recursion/SumOfdigits.java.complexity: Time O(log n) in the value of n (one call per digit), space O(log n).

src/Recursion/ReverseNumber.java.statement: Reverse the digits of an integer, so 1234 becomes 4321, using recursion.
src/Recursion/ReverseNumber.java.teaches: Carrying an accumulator through recursive calls. Unlike digit-sum, order matters here, so you multiply the running result by 10 before adding each new digit.
src/Recursion/ReverseNumber.java.complexity: Time O(log n), space O(log n).

src/Recursion/CountNumberOfZero.java.statement: Count how many zero digits appear in a non-negative integer, using recursion.
src/Recursion/CountNumberOfZero.java.teaches: The same digit-peeling skeleton as digit-sum, but the accumulator increments conditionally. Good practice at keeping recursion state in a parameter instead of a field.
src/Recursion/CountNumberOfZero.java.complexity: Time O(log n), space O(log n).

src/Recursion/FibonacciNumber.java.teaches: Naive tree recursion: fib(n) makes two calls, so the call tree has about 2^n nodes. This is the standard motivating example for memoisation and DP — worth timing against an iterative version to feel the difference.
src/Recursion/FibonacciNumber.java.statement: Return the nth Fibonacci number, where each term is the sum of the two before it and the sequence starts 0, 1.

src/Recursion/TrianglePattern.java.statement: Print a triangle of stars using only recursion — no for or while loops. The row and column counters live in the parameters.
src/Recursion/TrianglePattern.java.teaches: Replacing nested loops with two mutually recursive parameters. The trick is deciding whether to recurse 'along the row' or 'down to the next row' first, since that ordering is what produces the shape.
src/Recursion/TrianglePattern.java.complexity: Time O(n^2) characters printed, space O(n) stack depth.

src/Recursion/CheckPalindrome.java.statement: Check whether a string reads the same forwards and backwards, using recursion. Compare the character at index i with the character at index length - i - 1 and recurse inwards.
src/Recursion/CheckPalindrome.java.teaches: Two-pointer logic expressed recursively. Only half the string needs visiting, and any single mismatch can return false immediately without unwinding further work.
src/Recursion/CheckPalindrome.java.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the call stack.

src/Recursion/PalindromeOrNot.java.statement: Decide whether a number is a palindrome by reversing its digits recursively and comparing the reversal with the original.
src/Recursion/PalindromeOrNot.java.teaches: Reusing digit reversal as a building block. Contrast with the string version: numbers have no random access, so you must rebuild the value rather than index into it.
src/Recursion/PalindromeOrNot.java.complexity: Time O(log n), space O(log n).

src/Recursion/ReverseArray.java.statement: Reverse an array in place using recursion. Swap the element at index i with the element at index length - i - 1, then recurse on i + 1, stopping at the midpoint.
src/Recursion/ReverseArray.java.teaches: In-place mutation through recursion, and why the base case is index >= length / 2 rather than index >= length — recursing past the middle would swap every pair back and undo the work.

src/Recursion/LinearSearch.java.statement: Find the index of a target value in an array by checking one element per recursive call, returning -1 when the array is exhausted.
src/Recursion/LinearSearch.java.teaches: The simplest recursive search, and a useful baseline: it establishes the O(n) cost that binary search improves on when the array is sorted.

src/Recursion/BinarySearch.java.statement: Search a sorted array for a target and return its index, or -1 if absent, expressed recursively: compare against the middle element and recurse into whichever half can still contain the target.
src/Recursion/BinarySearch.java.teaches: The recursive shape of binary search. Compute mid as start + (end - start) / 2 rather than (start + end) / 2 to avoid integer overflow on large bounds.
src/Recursion/BinarySearch.java.complexity: Time O(log n), space O(log n) stack — the iterative form is O(1) space.

src/Recursion/SearchInRotatedArray.java.statement: Search a sorted array that has been rotated at some unknown pivot, in O(log n), using recursion.
src/Recursion/SearchInRotatedArray.java.teaches: At every midpoint one of the two halves is guaranteed to be sorted. Identify which, test whether the target lies inside that sorted half's range, and recurse accordingly.
src/Recursion/SearchInRotatedArray.java.complexity: Time O(log n), space O(log n).

src/Recursion/ArraySortedOrNot.java.statement: Return whether an array is sorted in non-decreasing order, using recursion: if the first pair is in order, the answer depends only on the rest of the array.
src/Recursion/ArraySortedOrNot.java.teaches: Recursion over a shrinking suffix, and short-circuiting — the first out-of-order pair ends the whole computation.

src/Recursion/RemoveAInString.java.statement: Build a new string with every occurrence of the character 'a' removed, using recursion and no loops.
src/Recursion/RemoveAInString.java.teaches: String building through recursion: at each step either keep the current character or skip it, then recurse on the remainder. The same skip-or-keep choice is the basis of subsequence and subset generation.
src/Recursion/RemoveAInString.java.complexity: Time O(n) calls; O(n^2) overall if each step concatenates a new String, since Java strings are immutable.

src/Recursion/RemoveStringFromString.jav.statement: Remove every occurrence of a given substring (such as "apple") from a target string, using recursion.
src/Recursion/RemoveStringFromString.jav.teaches: Generalising single-character removal to a multi-character pattern, which needs a startsWith check and a jump of the pattern's whole length rather than a single index step.
src/Recursion/RemoveStringFromString.jav.complexity: Time O(n x m) for target length n and pattern length m.

src/Recursion/SubSequence.java.statement: Print or collect every subsequence of a string — each character is either included or skipped, preserving the original order.
src/Recursion/SubSequence.java.teaches: The include/exclude recursion tree that generates 2^n results. This is the pattern every subset, combination and partition problem is built from.
src/Recursion/SubSequence.java.complexity: Time O(n x 2^n), space O(n) stack plus output.

src/Recursion/Permutation.java.statement: Generate all permutations of a string by inserting the current character at every position of each permutation built so far.
src/Recursion/Permutation.java.teaches: The insert-into-every-position formulation of permutations, which differs from the swap-based one. Contrast with LeetcodePermutation.java in this same folder.
src/Recursion/Permutation.java.complexity: Time O(n x n!), space O(n x n!) for the output.

src/Recursion/BubbleSort.java.statement: Bubble sort written recursively: one recursive pass bubbles the largest remaining element to the end, then the problem shrinks by one.
src/Recursion/BubbleSort.java.teaches: Turning the outer and inner loops of an iterative sort into two recursion parameters. Useful for seeing that loops and recursion are interchangeable.

src/Recursion/SelectionSort.java.statement: Selection sort written recursively: find the maximum of the unsorted prefix, swap it into place at the end, then recurse on the smaller prefix.
src/Recursion/SelectionSort.java.teaches: Selection sort does O(n^2) comparisons but only O(n) swaps, which matters when moving an element is far more expensive than comparing two.
src/Recursion/SelectionSort.java.complexity: Time O(n^2) comparisons, O(n) swaps, space O(n) stack.

src/Recursion/MergeSort.java.statement: Sort an array by recursively splitting it in half, sorting each half, and merging the two sorted halves back together.
src/Recursion/MergeSort.java.teaches: The archetypal divide-and-conquer sort. The merge step is where the work happens, and it is stable. Unlike quicksort it guarantees O(n log n) regardless of input, at the cost of O(n) extra space.
src/Recursion/MergeSort.java.complexity: Time O(n log n) always, space O(n).

src/Recursion/BackTracking/Maze.java.statement: Count the number of distinct paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of an n x m grid when you may only move right or down.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/Maze.java.teaches: The simplest backtracking counter: two recursive branches, no state to undo. The answer is the binomial coefficient C(n+m-2, n-1), so it is a good check that a brute-force count matches a closed form.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/Maze.java.complexity: Time O(2^(n+m)) without memoisation, space O(n+m) stack.

src/Recursion/BackTracking/MazePathDiago.statement: Count paths across a grid when diagonal movement is allowed in addition to right and down.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/MazePathDiago.teaches: Adding a third branch to the recursion multiplies the search space. Shows how branching factor, not depth, dominates backtracking cost.

src/Recursion/BackTracking/MazePrintingP.statement: Print the actual route of every path across the grid, not just how many there are, by carrying the path built so far through the recursion.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/MazePrintingP.teaches: The difference between counting and enumerating: enumeration needs a path accumulator that is appended on the way down and restored on the way back up.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/MazePrintingP.complexity: Time O(2^(n+m)) paths, each O(n+m) to print.

src/Recursion/BackTracking/PathWithObsta.statement: Count paths across a grid where some cells are blocked and may not be entered.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/PathWithObsta.teaches: Guarding the recursion with a validity check before descending. This is where backtracking starts to pay off over closed-form counting, since obstacles break the symmetry.

src/Recursion/BackTracking/AllPathsWithO.statement: Enumerate every path through a grid with blocked cells, moving in all permitted directions and marking cells as visited so a path never revisits itself.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/AllPathsWithO.teaches: Full backtracking: mark the cell, recurse, then unmark it on the way out. Forgetting the unmark is the single most common backtracking bug — it silently loses valid paths.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/AllPathsWithO.complexity: Time exponential in the number of free cells, space O(n x m).

src/Recursion/BackTracking/PrintMatrixPa.statement: Print paths through a matrix, tracking the route taken and the cells currently on the path.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/PrintMatrixPa.teaches: Combining a path accumulator with a visited marker, and printing the board state at each solution — the same scaffolding the N-Queens and Sudoku solvers use.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/PrintMatrixPa.complexity: Exponential in the number of cells.

src/Recursion/BackTracking/NKnights.java.statement: Place N knights on an N x N chessboard so that no knight attacks another, and count or print the valid arrangements.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/NKnights.java.teaches: Backtracking with a non-linear attack pattern. Unlike queens, a knight's threats are eight fixed offsets, so the safety check is a small explicit list rather than a row/column/diagonal scan.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/NKnights.java.complexity: Exponential; heavy pruning from the safety check.

src/Recursion/BackTracking/SudokuSolver..statement: Fill a partially completed 9x9 Sudoku grid so every row, column and 3x3 box contains the digits 1-9 exactly once.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/SudokuSolver..teaches: Constraint-propagating backtracking: try a digit, recurse, and reset the cell to empty if the branch fails. Compare with LeetcodeSudokuSolver.java in this folder.
src/Recursion/BackTracking/SudokuSolver..complexity: Exponential in the worst case, but real puzzles prune to near-instant.

src/Sorting/BubbleSort.java.statement: Sort an array by repeatedly comparing adjacent elements and swapping them when out of order, so each pass pushes the largest remaining element to the end.
src/Sorting/BubbleSort.java.teaches: Iterative bubble sort, and the early-exit optimisation: if a pass performs no swaps the array is already sorted, which makes the best case O(n). Compare with the recursive version in Recursion/BubbleSort.java.
src/Sorting/BubbleSort.java.complexity: Time O(n^2) worst and average, O(n) best with early exit. Space O(1). Stable.

src/Sorting/SelectionSort.java.statement: Sort an array by repeatedly selecting the largest (or smallest) element of the unsorted region and placing it at its final position.
src/Sorting/SelectionSort.java.teaches: Minimising writes: exactly n-1 swaps regardless of input. Preferable when writes are expensive, e.g. on flash storage. Compare with Recursion/SelectionSort.java.
src/Sorting/SelectionSort.java.complexity: Time O(n^2) always, space O(1). Not stable.

src/Sorting/InsertionSort.java.statement: Sort an array by taking each element in turn and inserting it into its correct place among the already-sorted elements before it.
src/Sorting/InsertionSort.java.teaches: Why insertion sort is the sort of choice for small or nearly-sorted inputs, and why real library sorts (including Java's) fall back to it below a size threshold. Adaptive and stable.
src/Sorting/InsertionSort.java.complexity: Time O(n^2) worst, O(n) on nearly-sorted input. Space O(1). Stable.

src/Sorting/QuickSort.java.teaches: Partitioning in place around a pivot, with no extra array — this is what makes quicksort faster than merge sort in practice despite the same average bound. The pivot choice is everything: taking the first element degrades to O(n^2) on already-sorted input, which is the case worth remembering in an interview.
src/Sorting/QuickSort.java.complexity: Time O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst. Space O(log n) stack. Not stable.
src/Sorting/QuickSort.java.statement: Sort an array in place by choosing a pivot, partitioning the array so that everything smaller sits to the pivot's left and everything larger to its right, then recursing on both sides.

src/Sorting/CyclicSort.java.statement: Sort an array containing the numbers 1..n (each exactly once) in O(n) time by repeatedly swapping each value directly to the index where it belongs.
src/Sorting/CyclicSort.java.teaches: The key insight behind a whole family of problems: when values are a known permutation of 1..n, index i should hold value i+1, so you can place elements directly instead of comparing them. Every 'find the missing/duplicate number in 1..n' problem in this folder is built on it.

src/BinarySearch/FloorProblem.java.statement: Given a sorted array and a target, return the floor of the target: the largest element less than or equal to it. Return -1 when every element is larger.
src/BinarySearch/FloorProblem.java.teaches: Binary search that answers a question the target may not satisfy exactly. When the loop ends, `end` has settled on the floor — recognising which pointer holds the answer is the whole skill.

src/BinarySearch/CielingProblem.java.statement: Given a sorted array and a target, return the ceiling of the target: the smallest element greater than or equal to it.
src/BinarySearch/CielingProblem.java.teaches: The mirror image of the floor problem — here `start` holds the answer when the loop ends. Together, floor and ceiling are the template for insert-position and range-boundary problems.

src/BinarySearch/BinarySearchRotateArray.statement: Decide whether a target exists in a rotated sorted array that may contain duplicate values.
src/BinarySearch/BinarySearchRotateArray.teaches: Duplicates break the usual guarantee that one half is sorted: when arr[start], arr[mid] and arr[end] are all equal you cannot tell which side to discard, so you shrink both ends by one. That single case is what pushes the worst case to O(n).
src/BinarySearch/BinarySearchRotateArray.complexity: Time O(log n) average, O(n) worst when values repeat. Space O(1).

src/BinarySearch/FindTargetInInfiniteArr.statement: Search a sorted array of unknown or unbounded length for a target, without being told where it ends.
src/BinarySearch/FindTargetInInfiniteArr.teaches: Exponential range-doubling: start with a window of size 2 and double it until the target falls inside, then binary search that window. Finding the range costs O(log n) and so does the search, so the total is still logarithmic.

src/BinarySearch/RotateCount.java.statement: Find how many times a sorted array has been rotated, which is the index of its smallest element.
src/BinarySearch/RotateCount.java.teaches: The rotation count equals the pivot index, so this reduces to finding the minimum in a rotated array. Recognising that reduction is the point.

src/BinarySearch/MatrixTarget.java.statement: Search for a target in a 2D matrix whose rows are sorted, returning its row and column, or [-1,-1] when absent.
src/BinarySearch/MatrixTarget.java.teaches: Narrowing to a candidate row first, then binary searching within it. Compare with SortedMatrixTarget.java, which exploits a stronger sortedness guarantee.
src/BinarySearch/MatrixTarget.java.complexity: Time O(log n + log m), space O(1).

src/BinarySearch/SortedMatrixTarget.java.statement: Search a matrix sorted both left-to-right along each row and top-to-bottom down each column.
src/BinarySearch/SortedMatrixTarget.java.teaches: The staircase walk: start at a corner where one direction increases and the other decreases (top-right or bottom-left), and each comparison eliminates a whole row or column. O(n + m) with no binary search at all.

src/StackAndQueue/CustomStack.java.statement: Implement a fixed-capacity stack over a plain array, supporting push, pop, peek, isEmpty and isFull, and raising an error on underflow or overflow.
src/StackAndQueue/CustomStack.java.teaches: Stack mechanics from scratch: a single `pointer` index is the whole data structure. Establishes the invariant that pointer always indexes the top element.

src/StackAndQueue/DynamicStack.java.statement: Extend the fixed-capacity stack so that pushing onto a full stack doubles the backing array instead of failing.
src/StackAndQueue/DynamicStack.java.teaches: Amortised analysis: a single push can cost O(n) when it triggers a copy, but doubling makes the average over many pushes O(1). This is exactly how ArrayList grows.
src/StackAndQueue/DynamicStack.java.complexity: Push amortised O(1), worst case O(n) on resize. Pop and peek O(1).

src/StackAndQueue/CustomQueue.java.statement: Implement a fixed-capacity queue over an array with insert and remove operations in FIFO order.
src/StackAndQueue/CustomQueue.java.teaches: Why the naive array queue is unsatisfying: removing from the front either shifts every element (O(n)) or leaks unusable space at the head. That problem is what CircularQueue solves.
src/StackAndQueue/CustomQueue.java.complexity: Insert O(1); remove O(n) if shifting.

src/StackAndQueue/CircularQueue.java.statement: Implement a queue over a fixed array that wraps around, reusing slots freed at the front so no space is wasted and both ends are O(1).
src/StackAndQueue/CircularQueue.java.teaches: Modular index arithmetic — front and end advance with % capacity. The subtle part is distinguishing full from empty when both indices coincide, which is why a separate size counter is kept.

src/StackAndQueue/DynamicQueue.java.statement: A circular queue that grows its backing array when full rather than rejecting the insert.
src/StackAndQueue/DynamicQueue.java.teaches: Resizing a circular buffer is harder than resizing a linear one: the elements must be unwrapped into their logical order as they are copied, not copied blindly.
src/StackAndQueue/DynamicQueue.java.complexity: Insert amortised O(1), O(n) on resize.

src/StackAndQueue/TwoStacks.java.teaches: Hosting two independent stacks in one array by growing them toward each other from opposite ends. Space is only exhausted when the combined size fills the array, which beats splitting the array in half.
src/StackAndQueue/TwoStacks.java.statement: Implement two independent stacks inside a single fixed-size array, so that neither runs out of room while the other still has free space.

src/StackAndQueue/StackException.java.statement: A small checked exception type used to signal stack underflow and overflow in the custom stack implementations.
src/StackAndQueue/StackException.java.teaches: Defining a domain-specific exception by extending Exception and forwarding a message to super. Checked (rather than runtime) so callers are forced to handle the empty-stack case.

src/StackAndQueue/StackMain.java.statement: Driver that exercises the custom stack implementations in this package.
src/StackAndQueue/StackMain.java.teaches: Scratch harness — read it alongside CustomStack and DynamicStack to see the operations in sequence.

src/StackAndQueue/QueueMain.java.statement: Driver that exercises the custom queue implementations in this package.
src/StackAndQueue/QueueMain.java.teaches: Scratch harness — read it alongside CustomQueue, CircularQueue and DynamicQueue.

src/StackAndQueue/InbuildExamples.java.statement: Worked examples of Java's built-in Stack, Queue, ArrayDeque and PriorityQueue classes and their method names.
src/StackAndQueue/InbuildExamples.java.teaches: Which JDK class to actually reach for in an interview, and the naming traps: Stack uses push/pop/peek, Queue uses offer/poll/peek, and Deque can serve as either. ArrayDeque is preferred over the legacy synchronised Stack.

src/LinkedList/Basic/LinkedList.java.statement: A singly linked list built from scratch: insert at head, at tail and at an index; delete from either end or by index; find a value; and print the chain.
src/LinkedList/Basic/LinkedList.java.teaches: Pointer surgery. Keeping an explicit tail reference makes append O(1) instead of O(n), and every insert or delete is really the same three steps: find the node before the target, rewire its next, adjust size.
src/LinkedList/Basic/LinkedList.java.complexity: Insert/delete at head O(1), at tail O(1) with a tail pointer, by index O(n). Search O(n).

src/LinkedList/Basic/DoublyLinkedList.ja.statement: A doubly linked list where each node holds both next and previous references, supporting insertion and deletion from either end and at an index.
src/LinkedList/Basic/DoublyLinkedList.ja.teaches: The prev pointer buys O(1) deletion given only a node reference, at the cost of an extra field and twice the rewiring per operation — every insert must fix four links, and missing one silently corrupts the list.
src/LinkedList/Basic/DoublyLinkedList.ja.complexity: Insert/delete at either end O(1), by index O(n).

src/LinkedList/Basic/CircularLinkedList..statement: A circular linked list in which the last node points back to the head instead of to null.
src/LinkedList/Basic/CircularLinkedList..teaches: Traversal termination changes completely: you cannot test for null, so you loop until you return to the head. This structure suits round-robin scheduling and any repeating rotation.
src/LinkedList/Basic/CircularLinkedList..complexity: Insert O(1) at head with a tail reference; delete and search O(n).

src/LinkedList/Basic/Main.java.statement: Driver exercising the singly linked list implementation.

src/LinkedList/Basic/DoublyLLMain.java.statement: Driver exercising the doubly linked list implementation.

src/LinkedList/Basic/CicularLLMain.java.statement: Driver exercising the circular linked list implementation.

src/Trees/BinaryTree.java.statement: Build a binary tree interactively and traverse it in pre-order, in-order and post-order, plus a formatted display of its structure.
src/Trees/BinaryTree.java.teaches: The three depth-first orders differ only in where you place the visit relative to the two recursive calls. In-order on a BST yields sorted output, which is the fact most tree problems exploit.
src/Trees/BinaryTree.java.complexity: Each traversal O(n) time, O(h) stack for height h.

src/Trees/BinarySearchTree.java.statement: A binary search tree supporting insert, search, balance checking and the three traversals, maintaining the invariant that every left subtree holds smaller values and every right subtree larger ones.
src/Trees/BinarySearchTree.java.teaches: Why the BST invariant makes search O(h), and why h is not automatically log n — inserting already-sorted data degenerates the tree into a linked list with O(n) lookups. That degeneration is exactly what AVLTree.java fixes.
src/Trees/BinarySearchTree.java.complexity: Insert and search O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate.

src/Trees/AVLTree.java.statement: A self-balancing binary search tree that restores balance after each insertion by rotating, keeping every node's subtree heights within one of each other.
src/Trees/AVLTree.java.teaches: The four rotation cases (left-left, left-right, right-right, right-left) and how tracking height per node lets you detect imbalance in O(1). This is what guarantees O(log n) worst case rather than merely average.
src/Trees/AVLTree.java.complexity: Insert and search O(log n) guaranteed.

src/Trees/SegmentTree.java.statement: A segment tree over an array supporting range-sum queries and point updates, each in logarithmic time, by storing every interval's aggregate in a binary tree of intervals.
src/Trees/SegmentTree.java.teaches: The trade prefix sums cannot make: prefix sums give O(1) queries but O(n) updates, while a segment tree gives O(log n) for both. Reach for it when the data changes between queries. Compare with PrefixSum/RangeSumQuery.java.
src/Trees/SegmentTree.java.complexity: Build O(n), query O(log n), update O(log n), space O(4n).

src/Heap/HeapLecture.java.statement: A generic binary min-heap over an ArrayList, supporting insert, remove-min and a full heap sort, with up-heap and down-heap restoring the heap property after each change.
src/Heap/HeapLecture.java.teaches: The array-as-tree trick: for index i the parent is (i-1)/2, children are 2i+1 and 2i+2 — no node objects needed. Insert sifts up, remove swaps the last element to the root and sifts down. This is what PriorityQueue is underneath.
src/Heap/HeapLecture.java.complexity: Insert and remove O(log n), peek O(1), heap sort O(n log n).

src/Leetcode/AlternatingSubstring.java.teaches: Scanning for runs where adjacent characters alternate. The pattern is to walk once and reset a counter whenever the alternation breaks, tracking the best run seen.
src/Leetcode/AlternatingSubstring.java.statement: Work with substrings whose adjacent characters always differ (an alternating pattern), scanning the input to measure or count such runs.

src/LeetcodeContest/LargestEvenNumber.ja.teaches: Contest problem — the statement was not pasted into the source. The code is the record of the approach; open the contest link if one is present.

src/LeetcodeContest/MaxCapacityWithinBud.teaches: Contest problem — the statement was not pasted into the source. The shape (maximise a quantity subject to a budget) usually points at binary search on the answer.

src/Main.java.statement: IntelliJ's generated starter file, kept only so the module compiles.
src/Main.java.teaches: Not a problem. Notable only as an example of a JDK 25 implicitly declared class: no class declaration, an instance void main(), and IO.println.

src/TestMain.java.statement: Scratch file for trying language features.

src/Recursion/DiceProblem.java.statement: Count the number of distinct ways to reach a target sum by rolling a dice, where each roll contributes 1 to 6. Order matters, so 1 then 2 is a different way from 2 then 1.
src/Recursion/DiceProblem.java.teaches: Branching recursion with a variable branching factor: at each step you try every face that does not overshoot the target. This is the unbounded-coin-change / staircase pattern, and it is the natural place to introduce memoisation.
src/Recursion/DiceProblem.java.complexity: Time O(6^n) naive, O(n) with memoisation. Space O(n) stack.
